strengths: Addresses a practical NLP question: how much labelled data makes specialising a smaller model competitive with prompting a general model. Examining learning curves across label budgets provides useful information beyond comparisons at only few-shot and full-data settings.

The experimental coverage is substantial: eight datasets, eight models and four approaches, with 100 fine-tuning runs, 20 runs for most alternatives and 10 for GPT. Reporting variation across runs and disaggregated results is valuable.

The multiclass results support the narrower finding that small tuned classifiers can surpass the tested general-model baselines with tens or hundreds of examples. The manuscript provides a source-code link, substantial experimental details and explicit discussion of limitations.
weaknesses: The headline average of 100 labels is not traceable to a clearly defined aggregation. For the fine-tuning comparisons in Table 1, the arithmetic means across datasets are 680 labels against the best prompting baseline and approximately 1,941 against the best in-context baseline. Other comparisons could produce different averages, but the manuscript must specify the included model pairs, weighting and treatment of unreached thresholds. This ambiguity directly limits the central practical recommendation.

The second break-even point has an overstated statistical interpretation. Non-overlap of mean ± one standard deviation is a descriptive heuristic, not a worst-case bound or a calibrated guarantee that one model will rarely lose. The claimed 100–200% increase consequently depends on an unjustified robustness criterion. Estimate paired probabilities of superiority or relevant performance quantiles with uncertainty, and distinguish run-to-run variability from uncertainty about average performance.

The prompting baselines require validation. Table 2 describes BoolQ as determining whether a passage contains an answer, whereas its target is the yes/no answer to the question given the passage. This mismatch can distort comparisons with supervised models. Additionally, one prompt engineered on Mistral is reused across models despite acknowledged prompt sensitivity. Correct task formulations, model-appropriate formatting and a limited held-out prompt sensitivity study are needed.

Label accounting and configuration selection are insufficiently specified. Appendix A creates a 20% validation split and uses early stopping without explaining whether validation labels fall within the reported budget. The paper also reports the best models, quantisation variants and demonstration counts without establishing which data select them. Uncounted validation supervision would undermine the annotation-budget interpretation; selection using test results would bias the reported comparisons. Specify and enforce a selection protocol within the stated label budget.

Several secondary conclusions exceed the evidence. Cross-family comparisons do not isolate model size from architecture and training history, and Figure 3 does not establish the proposed pretraining-contamination explanation. The negligible-quantisation claim also needs qualification: Figure 6 shows Zephyr's BoolQ prompting performance falling from approximately 68 to 41 macro-F1 under quantisation. These findings warrant conclusions tied to the evaluated configurations.

The compute-efficiency argument is underdeveloped. Table 3 supplies single FLOP totals without the training sizes and token counts needed to reproduce them, and does not establish comparable compute across the label-budget sweep. Bit-width-normalised FLOPs alone do not demonstrate runtime or deployment-cost savings. A fully specified cost model or measurements are needed to support the stronger resource-allocation recommendations.

Important reproducibility ambiguities remain. Appendix D's statement that larger general models were evaluated at a single 1,000-label setting needs reconciliation with the label-budget methodology. Several exact checkpoint identifiers, LoRA settings, quantisation details, output-to-label parsing rules and threshold-estimation procedures are unspecified in the manuscript. Together with the baseline and statistical issues, these warrant targeted reruns and reanalysis before a clear Findings recommendation.
